what_it_is.prose: The Multirole Transport Aircraft (MTA), also designated Il-214, was a planned medium military airlifter of roughly the 20-tonne payload class that India and Russia intended to co-develop. It was structured through the joint venture Multirole Transport Aircraft Ltd (MTAL), with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited holding 50% and Russia's United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) and Rosoboronexport holding 25% each. The concept dated back to protocols from the early 2000s, with a general (tripartite) contract signed in May 2012 and each side committing about $300 million for the first phase; a first flight was originally targeted around 2017. India planned to acquire around 45 aircraft (Russia about 100, with export ambitions) to replace its ageing Antonov An-32 fleet. The programme stalled and was effectively shelved by early 2016: the Indian Air Force objected to the proposed Russian PD-14M turbofan engine and its altitude performance, the two sides could not agree on cost as Russia sought increased development funding, there were design and workshare disputes, and internal Russian coordination problems slowed progress. India's decision to extend the service life of ~104 An-32s through a mid-life upgrade further reduced the urgency. No prototype was ever built or flown. India subsequently pursued the Airbus C-295 for its medium-transport requirement — ordering 56 aircraft with a large share built in India by Tata Advanced Systems at Vadodara — and later saw other proposals (such as the Embraer/Mahindra C-390) for its transport needs. The Atlas records the MTA as a historically relevant but cancelled India–Russia programme.

deployments_procurement.summary: The MTA never reached production or service — no aircraft were procured or delivered. It was a development joint venture (MTAL) intended to yield ~45 aircraft for India and ~100 for Russia to replace the An-32, but it was shelved around 2016. India instead upgraded its An-32 fleet and procured the Airbus C-295.

import_dependencies.summary: As a would-be joint Indo-Russian aircraft, the MTA's critical dependency was the collaboration itself — and its central technical sticking point was propulsion. The Indian Air Force's objection to the Russian PD-14M turbofan (particularly altitude performance) was a key reason the programme collapsed, illustrating engine-import dependence as a decisive risk in Indo-Russian co-development.

items.note: IAF objected to the PD-14M and its altitude performance; a primary cause of the programme's collapse.
Cost escalation demands, design disputes and internal Russian coordination problems stalled the JV.
